title: A Houston Methodist study finds its case managers beat the hospital's AI at predicting discharge dates on the last day
summary: JAMA Network Open published a quality improvement study on September 3rd, 2026 comparing discharge dates produced by a commercial AI tool built into Houston Methodist Hospital's electronic health record against dates estimated by the hospital's own case managers. The study covered inpatient encounters discharged between August 1st, 2023 and February 28th, 2024. At admission the two were close. Nearer to discharge, which is when the answer is used to plan a bed, the case managers were substantially more accurate. The authors are at the Texas A and M School of Engineering Medicine in Houston and in the Department of Medicine at Houston Methodist Hospital. The study names no vendor and no product. It reports estimation accuracy rather than any effect on a patient, and says so.

public_access.how: The study is published open access and can be read in full, with its methods and its table of results. A hospital's choice of a clinical software tool is not a public proceeding and there is no room a resident can attend.

claims.text: The study reports how often each method landed within a day of the true discharge date in the last 24 hours.
claims.verbatim_quote: At 24 hours, 79.5% of case manager estimations fell within 1 day vs 37.9% for AI estimations
claims.source_title: JAMA Network Open, Artificial Intelligence vs Case Manager Estimation of Discharge Dates for Hospitalized Patients

claims.text: The study states where the encounters came from and over what period.
claims.verbatim_quote: This quality improvement study included inpatient encounters at Houston Methodist Hospital with discharge dates between August 1, 2023, and February 28, 2024.
claims.source_title: JAMA Network Open, Artificial Intelligence vs Case Manager Estimation of Discharge Dates for Hospitalized Patients

claims.text: The study describes what produced the AI dates, without naming a vendor or a product.
claims.verbatim_quote: Artificial intelligence–estimated discharge dates were generated by a commercial clinician-assisted tool integrated with the EHR.
claims.source_title: JAMA Network Open, Artificial Intelligence vs Case Manager Estimation of Discharge Dates for Hospitalized Patients

claims.text: The study states its own finding, and names when an accurate estimate actually matters.
claims.verbatim_quote: This quality improvement study found that AI-estimated discharge was comparable to usual care at admission but outperformed by case managers as discharge approached (when accurate estimations are most actionable for bed management).
claims.source_title: JAMA Network Open, Artificial Intelligence vs Case Manager Estimation of Discharge Dates for Hospitalized Patients

claims.text: The study warns against reading the admission result as evidence the tool knows what a clinician knows.
claims.verbatim_quote: The strong admission correlation did not persist nearer discharge and should not be interpreted as evidence that the tool captured the same information clinicians use throughout the stay.
claims.source_title: JAMA Network Open, Artificial Intelligence vs Case Manager Estimation of Discharge Dates for Hospitalized Patients

claims.text: The study names the limitation that cuts hardest against its own headline, which is that the case managers' own estimates were visible to the people acting on them.
claims.verbatim_quote: Case manager estimates were part of usual care and visible to care teams, so they may be partly self-fulfilling and, thus, advantaged nearer discharge; AI estimations were accessible in the EHR but not enabled automatically.
claims.source_title: JAMA Network Open, Artificial Intelligence vs Case Manager Estimation of Discharge Dates for Hospitalized Patients

claims.text: The study says what would have to happen before anyone concludes the tool is worth its implementation.
claims.verbatim_quote: Whether the AI’s incremental accuracy in selected subgroups justifies the complexity of implementation warrants prospective, outcome-based evaluation.
claims.source_title: JAMA Network Open, Artificial Intelligence vs Case Manager Estimation of Discharge Dates for Hospitalized Patients

claims.text: The study reports the mean absolute error of each method at each of the three points it measured.
claims.verbatim_quote: Nearer to discharge, case managers vs AI were more accurate (48 hours: MAE, 1.29 [95% CI, 1.26-1.32] vs 1.59 [95% CI 1.57-1.61] days; 24 hours: MAE, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.96-1.01] vs 1.93 [95% CI, 1.91-1.95] days) (both P < .001).
claims.source_title: JAMA Network Open, Artificial Intelligence vs Case Manager Estimation of Discharge Dates for Hospitalized Patients

title: Lubbock heard a citizen petition for an 18 month data center moratorium and passed a resolution instead
summary: The Lubbock City Council held a public hearing on September 8th, 2026 on a citizen petition brought under the city charter, asking for an 18 month moratorium on high water use and high energy use data centers inside the city. The council did not adopt the petition's ordinance. It took up a separate resolution stating the council's desire that large scale data centers not be developed inside the municipal limits until the council has adopted regulations protecting public resources and public health and safety. A resolution states a desire and an ordinance states a rule, and the two items sat next to each other on the same agenda.

key_dates.note: Public hearing on the charter petition, and the resolution taken up beside it

public_access.how: The council meets in open session at Citizens Tower and posts its agendas. A resident can speak at a council meeting. Any regulation the resolution anticipates would come back to the council as an ordinance through further public proceedings.

claims.text: The agenda states what the public hearing was on, and under which part of the city charter it was held.
claims.verbatim_quote: Public Hearing - City Secretary: Conduct a public hearing in accordance with Chapter 1, Article IV, Section 1 of the City of Lubbock Charter, regarding an "18-month moratorium on high-water-use and high-energy-use data centers in the City of Lubbock, Lubbock County, Texas."
claims.source_title: City of Lubbock, Regular City Council Meeting agenda, September 8th, 2026

claims.text: The agenda states what the resolution beside it would do, and what it waits on.
claims.verbatim_quote: Resolution - City Council: Consider a resolution expressing the City Council's desire that large-scale data centers not be developed within the municipal limits of the City of Lubbock, until the City Council has adopted regulations protecting public resources and the public health and safety.
claims.source_title: City of Lubbock, Regular City Council Meeting agenda, September 8th, 2026

claims.text: A speaker at the hearing said the pause the petition asked for was not what she wanted.
claims.verbatim_quote: I don't want an 18-month moratorium. I want us to collectively say no to this.
claims.source_title: Fox 34, Lubbock City Council passes non binding resolution regarding data centers within city limits

title: The grid operator sets an October 6th workshop on how it would actually switch a large load off under Senate Bill 6
summary: ERCOT issued a market notice on September 2nd, 2026 setting a workshop for October 6th to present the deployment mechanics, the registration process and the draft revision requests for curtailing large loads under Senate Bill 6. The notice names the three provisions the bill put into the Public Utility Regulatory Act. One lets the commission require a large load co-located with an existing generation resource to reduce consumption during certain events. One lets the grid operator require a large load with backup generation serving at least half its load to curtail grid consumption to head off an emergency. One requires the commission to establish a large load demand management service. The workshop is the step where a legal authority becomes a registry and a piece of software.

key_dates.note: Workshop on the proposed large load curtailment framework

public_access.how: The market notice names the workshop, its date and its intended audience. The grid operator publishes its market notices to anyone, and the revision requests the workshop previews go through its own stakeholder process before they are filed.

claims.text: The notice states what the workshop will cover and when it is.
claims.verbatim_quote: On October 6, 2026 ERCOT will host a workshop to present the deployment mechanics, registration process, and draft revision requests for Large Load curtailment under Senate Bill 6 (SB6).

claims.text: The notice names who it is addressed to.
claims.verbatim_quote: Large Load Customers, Qualified Scheduling Entities, Transmission Service Providers and other interested stakeholders

claims.text: The notice states the three things the bill put into the statute, including the backup generation threshold.
claims.verbatim_quote: SB6 established several provisions in PURA related to Large Loads, including an authorization for the PUC to require Large Loads that co-locate with existing Generation Resources to reduce consumption during certain events (section 39.169); an authorization for ERCOT to require Large Loads with backup generation serving at least 50% of their load to curtail their grid consumption when necessary to mitigate actual or potential EEA conditions (section 37.0561(e)); and a requirement for the PUC to establish a large load demand management service (section 39.170).

claims.text: The notice states its own subject in one line.
claims.verbatim_quote: Workshop to share proposed operational framework for implementing SB6-related Large Load curtailments, including registration requirements
